intl.headline: The United States beat France 97–79 to win gold at the FIBA Women’s Basketball World Cup 2026
intl.deck: Breanna Stewart (the United States) 22, Dominique Malonga (France) 21 and Gabby Williams (France) 20 led the scoring and the United States won the offensive glass 12–6 to win gold in Berlin.
body: The United States won the gold medal at the FIBA Women’s Basketball World Cup 2026 at Uber Arena in Berlin on Sunday, September 13, beating France 97–79. France took silver.

Breanna Stewart led the United States with 22 points, 10 rebounds and 4 assists on 7-of-10 shooting. The clearest differences were the offensive glass (12 offensive rebounds to 6) and field-goal accuracy (56.3 percent to 48.1 percent).
France led 20–17 after the first quarter. The United States won the second quarter 26–25, and France led 45–43 at halftime.
The United States won the third quarter 30–12, leaving the score at 73–57 with a quarter to play. The United States then took the fourth quarter 24–22.
The United States won three of the four quarters, and the 18-point final margin was the widest of the game at any quarter break.

According to the play-by-play, the lead changed hands 6 times and the score was tied 6 times. The United States’ largest lead was 27 points, at 86–59 with 6:07 left in the fourth quarter. France’s biggest advantage was 14 points, in the second quarter.
France last led with 0:04 left in the second quarter, and the last tie came with 8:18 left in the third quarter; the United States did not trail after that.

The play-by-play shows where the United States pulled away for good: leading 55–51 with 4:45 left in the third quarter, the United States outscored France 31–8 over the next stretch to lead 86–59 with 6:07 left in the fourth quarter.
France turned the ball over 6 times in that stretch; the United States recorded 2 steals; and Caitlin Clark scored 9 and Kahleah Copper scored 5 of the 31 points in the run.

The United States’ margin came from measurable differences in the box score. The widest were the offensive glass (12 offensive rebounds to 6), field-goal accuracy (56.3 percent to 48.1 percent) and ball movement (21 assists to 15).
The United States also won the overall rebounding battle 38–25, and the 6-rebound edge on the offensive glass meant second chances France did not get.
The United States shot 36 of 64 (56.3 percent) from the field, 8 of 19 from three and 17 of 25 at the line; France went 26 of 54 (48.1 percent), 11 of 24 from three and 16 of 25 on free throws.
France held the edge in bench scoring (35 points to 24), which did not offset the rest.

Breanna Stewart was the United States’ most productive player, finishing with 22 points, 10 rebounds and 4 assists in 30 minutes. She shot 7 of 10 from the field and 8 of 9 at the line, with 2 turnovers. That was more than double the 11 points she had averaged over her previous five games of the tournament.

Jackie Young, a starter, added 18 points, 6 rebounds and 5 assists in 30 minutes on 7 of 14 from the field and 4 of 7 from three. She came in averaging 11.2 points over five earlier games of the tournament.

Chelsea Gray, a starter, added 12 points, 4 rebounds and 5 assists in 27 minutes on 5 of 9 from the field, 0 of 3 from three and 2 of 2 at the line. That was more than double the 4.4 points she had averaged over her previous five games of the tournament.

Kahleah Copper, a starter, added 15 points in 29 minutes on 5 of 9 from the field, 2 of 3 from three and 3 of 4 at the line. She came in averaging 7.8 points over five earlier games of the tournament.
Rhyne Howard contributed away from scoring with 4 steals.
The United States’ reserves scored 24 of the team’s 97 points; the France bench scored 35.
Dominique Malonga led France with 21 points and 6 rebounds on 8 of 12 from the field, 1 of 1 from three and 4 of 5 at the line; Gabby Williams added 20 points and Janelle Salaun added 7 points.
Carla Leite had 4 turnovers and Marine Johannes had 5 turnovers, part of a 16-turnover game for France.
France’s best period was the first quarter, won 20–17, but the United States won the quarters that followed.
Gold gives the United States first place at the FIBA Women’s Basketball World Cup 2026, played in Berlin; France takes silver.

In the group stage the United States beat China 94–61, beat Italy 55–52 and beat Czechia 105–64. It then beat Hungary 108–56 in the quarterfinal and beat Spain 76–66 in the semifinal. That 5–0 record became 6–0 with this win.

In the group stage France beat Hungary 99–53, beat South Korea 95–69 and beat Nigeria 111–56. It then beat China 90–61 in the quarterfinal and beat Germany 86–64 in the semifinal. France finishes the tournament 5–1.

Twenty players on current WNBA rosters appeared in this game, matched to their WNBA profiles by identical ESPN athlete IDs: Breanna Stewart (New York Liberty), Jackie Young (Las Vegas Aces), Chelsea Gray (Las Vegas Aces), Kahleah Copper (Phoenix Mercury), Caitlin Clark (Indiana Fever), Aliyah Boston (Indiana Fever), Rhyne Howard (Atlanta Dream), Napheesa Collier (Minnesota Lynx), Sonia Citron (Washington Mystics), Angel Reese (Atlanta Dream), Paige Bueckers (Dallas Wings) and Kiki Iriafen (Washington Mystics) for the United States; Dominique Malonga (Seattle Storm), Gabby Williams (Golden State Valkyries), Janelle Salaun (Golden State Valkyries), Valeriane Ayayi (Phoenix Mercury), Carla Leite (Portland Fire), Pauline Astier (New York Liberty), Leila Lacan (Connecticut Sun) and Marine Johannes (New York Liberty) for France.

Among them, Breanna Stewart finished with 22 points, 10 rebounds and 4 assists; Jackie Young finished with 18 points, 6 rebounds and 5 assists; Chelsea Gray finished with 12 points, 4 rebounds and 5 assists; and Kahleah Copper finished with 15 points.

body: The Chicago Sky’s last 10 completed games with a line in the source record went under the total 8 times. The misses were not marginal: the games averaged 171.2 points against an average total of 178.7, and four of them landed 10 or more points under. The source of the gap matters for whether it lasts: the Sky averaged 82.5 points in those games, 4.2 points below their season average of 86.7, while their opponents averaged 88.7, 1 point below the 89.7 they allow on the season. Most of the under run is the Sky’s own offense falling short.
Does it persist across the window? The five older games went under four times and the five most recent four times; the average total was 180.5 on the older games and 176.9 on the recent ones.
The exceptions: August 23 against the Fever, 203 points against a total of 187.5; August 10 at the Storm, 185 points against a total of 179.5.

Game by game: Aug 29 at NY 66–85 (151 points, total 181.5); Aug 25 at CON 81–87 (168 points, total 171.5); Aug 23 vs IND 90–113 (203 points, total 187.5); Aug 21 vs GS 73–70 (143 points, total 163.5); Aug 18 vs NY 93–86 (179 points, total 180.5); Aug 16 at SEA 82–80 (162 points, total 177.5); Aug 12 at GS 71–91 (162 points, total 166.5); Aug 10 at SEA 88–97 (185 points, total 179.5); Aug 8 vs IND 86–90 (176 points, total 191.5); Aug 5 vs LA 95–88 (183 points, total 187.5).
For the record, the same games went 4-6 against the spread.

The market now: PropBetEdge’s capture of Sep 13 (10 books, The Odds API) has the total for WSH at CHI on Sep 17 at 167.5, 11.2 below the run’s average total. Best prices: over 167.5 at -108 (FanDuel), under 167.5 at -108 (LowVig).
Across seven stored captures since Sep 11, that total has held at 167.5.
The Chicago Sky are 15-25, 4-6 over their last 10, scoring 86.7 points a game and allowing 89.7 on the season.
Next up is a home game against the Washington Mystics on Thursday, September 17; the Mystics are 24-16 and score 82.8 while allowing 83.
The opponent pulls the same way: the Mystics’ last 10 games averaged 170 total points, so a low number for that game is not only an adjustment to the Sky.

The case against the run: 10 games against one sportsbook’s totals is a small sample, and two of them went over, one by 15.5. Totals are set against both teams, so the next opponent changes the baseline, and the run describes past pricing rather than forecasting the next game.
